paragraphs.text: A [dark tea](dark:definition) made in 1983 from leaf grown in [Taiwan](taiwan:on-a-label). The label names only the island, not a mountain or a township, so where on it the leaf grew is not recorded. The island's tea first came across the strait from Fujian, and its trade is built on [oolong](taiwan:known-for).

Dark tea is leaf that, once heated and rolled, is left to change in warmth and moisture, and it is [made to be kept](dark:ageing). The trade values it more as the years pass, and storage sets the pace: kept cool and dry, the change is slow; kept warmer and more humid, it is faster. At forty-three years, this tea has had more than four decades of that change.

brewing.text: Dark tea takes boiling water. Its leaf is mature and dense, so it gives up its flavour slowly and is hard to overbrew. Rinse it first with boiling water and pour that off within seconds: the rinse wakes the leaf and washes off dust and any stale smell from storage, and an old tea may take a second rinse. In a small pot use plenty of leaf, about 7 grams to 120 ml, then steep very briefly at first and a little longer each time; a good dark tea gives many cups.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow cup with low bitterness and a deep red colour, often sweet and woody or earthy, sometimes with herbal or medicinal notes. A young dark tea can still smell of the pile or of storage; an aged one is usually redder, sweeter and thicker.
